result.summary: Pausanias walks through the Argive market area and describes monuments, including statues of Milichian and Nemean Zeus, tombs, and shrines. He tells how the Argive people destroyed the 1000 picked men after Bryas's crime, and how the poetess Telesilla led the women to defend Argos against Cleomenes.

scenes.title: Milichian Zeus and Bryas
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the statue of Milichian Zeus and explains its origin in the killing of the thousand picked men after Bryas outraged a maiden.
scenes.stakes: The maiden risks the vengeance of the thousand after blinding Bryas; the Argive people risk civil bloodshed.

scenes.title: Monuments of Argos
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists temples, tombs, statues of the Theban warriors, and the statue of Telesilla.

scenes.title: Telesilla and the Women
scenes.summary: After Cleomenes destroys the Argive army, Telesilla arms slaves and women, and the Lacedæmonians yield. This fulfils an oracle recorded by Herodotus.
scenes.stakes: Argos faces capture by the Lacedæmonians after losing its men.

notable_quotes.reason: The Spartans yield to the women, fearing dishonour whether they win or lose.

analysis.text: Monuments are explained by local stories of civil strife, piety and women's courage, tying the city's landmarks to its memory.
Pausanias combines local Argive tradition with literary sources like Æschylus and Herodotus, showing how civic memory shaped sacred topography.

language_notes.text: Effigy means statue or likeness; Creux is a boxer commemorated at Argos. "White stone" is marble or similar pale stone.
Expiation means ritual atonement for a crime, here to cleanse the pollution of killing fellow citizens. Milichian means "gentle" or "propitiated".
Cleobis and Bito were Argive brothers who yoked themselves to their mother's cart, a priestess of Hera, and pulled it to her temple.
Palamedes, a Greek hero at Troy, was credited in legend with inventing dice and other devices.
Aeschylus' play Seven against Thebes fixed the number of champions at seven, though Pausanias notes more contingents took part.
A cenotaph is an empty tomb honouring those buried elsewhere. Ilium is Troy.
Hypermnestra alone of Danaus' daughters spared her husband on the wedding night, against her father's order, and was tried for it.
Herodotus (6.77) records this oracle, given by the Pythian Priestess, the priestess of Apollo at Delphi.

context_notes.text: Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander, invaded the Peloponnese in 338 BC and limited Spartan territory in favour of Argos and others.
Phoroneus was a legendary early king of Argos, often called the first man or the discoverer of fire.
The women's mourning for Adonis was a ritual lament for the dying young god, a rite practised widely in Greece.
Othryades was the Spartan survivor of the famous Battle of the Champions between Argos and Sparta over Thyrea.
Cleomenes I, king of Sparta, defeated the Argives at Sepeia around 494 BC and burned the sacred grove where survivors had taken refuge.

literary_notes.text: Bryas is defined by insolence and the outrage on the maiden, preparing the story's violent outcome.
The outraged maiden, powerless by day, takes decisive revenge on the powerful captain while he sleeps.
One long, heaping sentence conveys the scale of Argive disaster, delaying its resolution until Cleomenes reaches the emptied city.
Spartans, famed warriors, retreat because victory over women would bring no glory and defeat only shame.
The oracle ambiguously predicted a female victory, which Pausanias now reads as fulfilled by Telesilla's women.
